environmentNote: The standing note that codex cannot be run on this machine is WRONG, and the seven skipping
tests were never evidence for it. Checked directly on 2026-08-23:
Real turns in these captures ran against the live API and returned real model output.
And the seven skips are not about codex's absence at all: `CodexIntegrationTests` opens with
opt-in gate, so those tests skip on a machine with a perfectly good codex — which is exactly
what happened here: the suite reported 1682 tests, 7 skipped, while codex was being driven
for real in another window. Two of the seven additionally check for an auth.json and would
skip on top of that. Recorded because 'seven tests skip, so codex must be missing' is an
inference that costs an hour and is wrong.
glyphs: **The prompt marker is NOT universal, and `ChoiceDialog.marker` must not be read as if it
were.** Three different characters are in play on this machine, and conflating any two of
claude's input box and dialog cursor   ❯   U+276F   HEAVY RIGHT-POINTING ANGLE QUOTATION
codex's input box and dialog cursor    ›   U+203A   SINGLE RIGHT-POINTING ANGLE QUOTATION
this machine's fish prompt             >   U+003E   plain ASCII greater-than
The separator after the marker differs too: claude draws U+00A0 (a non-breaking space, which
`InputBar.normalized` exists to cope with), codex draws a plain U+0020. Verified by codepoint
dump of the captured lines, not by eye — the two are indistinguishable on screen.
capturedBy: Five real codex sessions in a pty owned by the capture harness, at 136x45 with
TERM=xterm-ghostty, rendered from the pty byte stream by pyte 0.8.2 (an independent VT
emulator) and written with per-line trailing whitespace stripped. This is the same route,
and the same renderer, as the five pyte-only captures in Fixtures/Claude/.
Each ran under an isolated CODEX_HOME holding a copied auth.json (0600) and a config.toml of
two stanzas — `[features] hooks = false` and a trust entry for the throwaway workdir. The
operator's real ~/.codex/config.toml has an MCP server, three hook trust hashes, a
personality and four project-trust rows, NONE of which are in these captures.
No keystrokes were sent to produce any screen except the two that require one by
construction: `workspace-trust` is the untrusted-directory dialog on first run (no keystroke),
`tui-idle`/`tui-working`/`approval-command` were driven by a prompt passed on codex's own
command line (`codex [PROMPT]`, no keystroke), and `approval-command-row1` is
`approval-command` after exactly one Down arrow — the one capture here that a keypress
produced, and the reason it exists.
**These are the pyte render ONLY. They were NOT cross-checked through the Accessibility API,
and that is a real difference from the claude set.** `Fixtures/Claude/dialogs.captured.*`
records a cross-check: one of its screens was read out of a live Flight Deck tab through
`Ghostty.SurfaceView.accessibilityValue()`, which is `cachedScreenContents.get()` and is the
same `CachedValue<String>` object `TextInjecting.readViewport()` returns, and it matched the
pyte render character for character. That establishes the RENDERER as faithful, which is why
a pyte-only capture is worth something at all — but it was established for claude's screens,
not for these. Nothing here has been read through the API Flight Deck would actually use.
AXIsProcessTrusted() was never the blocker; the pty route was simply taken first and the
cross-check not reached. Anyone acting on these fixtures should do that pass first.
writerLock: **The app-server route for a TURN is closed, and this is now measured in both directions
rather than inherited.** `SessionStore.submitPrompt` asserts it; `CodexAdapter.prepare`
documents only the opposite direction. Probed on codex-cli 0.148.0 by driving a real
`codex app-server` over stdio (initialize with clientInfo, thread/start, thread/name/set,
thread/archive, thread/unarchive — exactly `CodexAdapter.prepare`'s sequence) with a real
`codex resume <id>` TUI alive in a pty holding the thread:
thread/resume  (same app-server connection)  -> -32600 'thread <id> already has an active writer'
turn/start     (same connection)             -> -32600 'thread not found: <id>'
thread/resume  (a SECOND app-server process) -> -32600 'thread <id> already has an active writer'
turn/start     (second process)              -> -32600 'thread not found: <id>'
thread/name/set(second process)              -> ok {}
and on codex's own stderr, from both server processes:
ERROR codex_core::session::session: failed to initialize thread persistence:
thread-store conflict: thread <id> already has an active writer
**The last row of that table is the point.** The metadata write is NOT gated by the writer
lock; LOADING the thread is, and a turn needs it loaded. That asymmetry is the precise reason
Flight Deck's rename ships over the app-server while a prompt cannot, and it is worth not
re-deriving. `turn/start` reports 'thread not found' rather than a lock error only because
the preceding `thread/resume` was refused, so the thread was never loaded into that server.
The control direction reproduced verbatim the string `CodexAdapter.prepare` quotes: with the
app-server holding the lock from `thread/start`, the pty `codex resume` died with
'thread/resume failed during TUI bootstrap: thread/resume failed: thread <id> already has an
active writer (code -32600)', and the archive/unarchive round trip released it.
NOT probed: `turn/steer` (in the schema; it presumably needs the thread loaded too, so almost
certainly the same lock, but that is an inference and not a measurement), and the
`codex remote-control` / `--remote` app-server-daemon route, which is a different architecture
rather than a revisit of this one.

route 'has no input box to read: InputBar.read locks onto the last line starting ❯, a glyph a

› (U+203A). `InputBar.read` tests `$0.first == marker` against U+276F, so on a codex screen it
matches NOTHING and returns nil. It cannot mistake codex's box for a draft, because it cannot
The near-miss the comment records was therefore never about codex. It is about the SHELL: a
codex tab sitting at a bare prompt, with a shell theme (pure, starship, spaceship) that draws
❯. That risk is real, is unchanged by anything here, and is about a shell rather than an
agent. This machine's own fish prompt draws '>' (U+003E) and would not trigger it.
A positive discriminator for codex does exist on screen: the status line directly below the
box — 'gpt-5.6-sol default · /private/tmp/codexcap/work', model then mode then cwd — which no
shell draws. It is in both tui-idle and tui-working.
codexInputLineShowsWhetherItIsBusy: REFUTED, and this is the caution that SURVIVES for typing. Compare tui-idle and tui-working:
the input line is byte-identical in both, '› Ask Codex to do anything', placeholder and all.
Codex keeps its box up and accepting during a turn. The only busy signal on screen is a
SEPARATE line above it, '◦ Working (3s • esc to interrupt)', whose seconds counter changes
So nothing that reads the input line alone can tell ready from working. Anything that gates
typing on 'the box looks idle' would be wrong mid-turn, every time.
And the placeholder/draft ambiguity is claude's exactly: '› Ask Codex to do anything' is a
HINT, rendered in the same shape as a real draft and differing only in colour, which
`ghostty_surface_read_text` does not return. `InputBar`'s own doc comment describes this
hazard for claude — kill first, compare `content` before and after, never guess from
appearance — and it transfers to codex unchanged.
codexDrawsChoiceDialogsTheInterlockCould: CONFIRMED, and codex's dialogs fit `ChoiceDialog`'s model MORE closely than claude's own do.
Every structural rule the interlock depends on holds, checked against approval-command,
approval-command-row1 and workspace-trust:
- optional marker, then `N.`, then a space, then the label
- contiguous numbering from 1; a blank line ends the run
- exactly one marker on screen, on the focused row; unfocused rows carry two leading
spaces and no marker
- the marker sits at column 1, the number at column 3, the label at column 6
- a stable footer: 'Press enter to confirm or esc to cancel' (approval), 'Press enter to
continue' (trust)
**The echoed-prompt trap exists here too, and the existing defence is exactly right for it.**
Codex echoes the submitted prompt with the same › and NO number, so a live session carries the
marker twice — see the '› Run the shell command: …' line in approval-command. `ChoiceDialog`'s
rule (a row is the marker AND a number AND a consecutively numbered neighbour) rejects that
echo for the same reason it rejects claude's.
`ChoiceDialog.parse` would work on these screens UNMODIFIED but for one constant:
`static let marker: Character = "❯"` would have to admit ›. That is production source and
was deliberately not touched by this capture. Note it is a widening, not a swap — claude's ❯
must keep working.
Two hazards confirmed, both matching claude's exactly:
- **Row 1 is a DURABLE GRANT** — 'Yes, and don't ask again for commands that start with
`mkdir -p …`'. So `answerPrompt`'s '.allow is the literal 0, and no arithmetic here can
reach a middle row' is as load-bearing for codex as for claude.
- **Row 2 is deny**, and the footer says so ('esc'), so the `.deny`-as-one-Escape path —
the one that needs no parse and works on a screen nothing can read — transfers directly.
One way codex is STRONGER than claude: its approval dialog prints the command verbatim on
screen ('$ mkdir -p /private/tmp/codexcap/work/newdir && echo made'), so there is real text to
confirm against. `answerPrompt`'s `.allow` arm documents that claude's permission dialog
carries NO label the Mac can read, which is why that interlock is 'STRUCTURALLY WEAKER' than
`.option`'s. Codex does not have that gap.

editingRule: Lines may be DROPPED, never EDITED. **In these five files, NOTHING was dropped.** Every line
of every file is byte-for-byte what codex drew on that grid, blank trailing rows included,
because a viewport IS its blank rows and a parser that scans upward has to meet them. All
five are exactly 45 lines, the height of the grid they were captured on.
That includes chrome a reader may be tempted to tidy and must not: the 'Update available!
0.148.0 -> 0.149.0' banner, the rotating 'Tip:' line (a different tip in each capture, which
is why they differ between files), and 'You have 1 usage limit reset available.' These are
part of what the screen really looks like, and a parser meets them.
**Scanned, and clean — this is a check, not an oversight.** Every captured screen was searched
for '/Users/nate', '.agents', 'auth', 'token', 'sk-' and '@gmail': ZERO hits. The preceding
capture in this directory leaked the operator's home path and an inventory of their private
~/.agents/skills, because codex reads ~/.agents/skills regardless of CODEX_HOME — see
rollout.captured.provenance.json. That leak was in rollout RECORDS (prompt assembly), and a
rendered TUI screen simply does not carry those; but it was searched for rather than assumed.
The only absolute paths present are /private/tmp/codexcap/work and .../work/newdir — the
throwaway workdir this capture made — plus the public URLs codex prints itself
(github.com/openai/codex, discord.gg/openai, chatgpt.com/codex). Nothing needed redaction, so
no shape is uncovered by a dropped line.
The raw pty byte streams are deliberately NOT in the repo, as with the claude captures: they
are not line-oriented, so nothing could be dropped from them without editing.
This is the same weak ground truth the other captures here are: it records what codex DID on
one day at one width, not what it DECLARES. There is no schema for a TUI.
Every fixture in this directory MUST be named *.captured.* to signal that it is verbatim
captured output, not authored. Tests reference captures by their documented name; if a test
cannot find its fixture, correct the lookup name in the test, never add an undocumented copy
under another name.
